editorial.title: [사설] 엉망이 된 세제개편안, 전면 재검토가 맞다
editorial.body: 입력 지난주 발표된 정부 세제개편안의 후폭풍이 거세다. 법제처 국민참여입법센터에 올라온 종합부동산세법과 소득세법 개정안에 대한 의견이 수천 건에 달한다. 세제개편안이 발표되자마자 조세 저항에 가까운 반발이 쏟아지는 것은 전례 없던 일이다. 특히 강남 초고가 주택에 거주하는 고령자와 비거주 1주택자의 반발이 거세다. 일부 초고가 주택은 연간 보유세가 수천만원까지 뛸 수 있어 오래전 집을 산 고령의 은퇴자는 감당하기 어렵다. 투기와 관계없는 고령의 장기 보유자들로선 무거운 징벌적 보유세에 대해 불만이 나올 수밖에 없을 것이다. 직장 변경, 질병 치료 등 정부가 예시한 비거주 1주택자의 예외 사유가 까다롭다는 불만도 있다. 손주 양육을 위해 살던 집을 세 주고 자녀 집 근처 주택을 임차한 이들도 있고, 유학이나 해외 근무로 장기간 집을 비워야 하는 이들도 있다. 사태가 심상치 않자 구윤철 경제부총리도 비거주 예외 요건을 최대한 신축적으로 검토하겠다고 물러섰다. 기존 절세 혜택이 줄어든 개인종합자산관리계좌(ISA)와 입법 취지에 역행하는 듯한 ‘주가 누르기’ 방지법도 청년층의 반발에 부닥쳤다. 결국 이재명 대통령의 질타를 받고 전면 재검토에 들어갔다. 세제 개편은 경제 운용의 큰 축인 데다 이미 당정 협의까지 마쳤다는 점에서 정책 발표 며칠 만에 대통령의 질타를 받는 장면은 매우 이례적이다. 여당 안에서도 “재경부 정신차려라”라는 비판이 나왔다. 당정 협의 이전에 청와대와의 조율도 마무리했을 터인데 이제까지 뭐하고 있다가 뒤늦게 나서는 것인지 납득이 가지 않는 대목이다. 청와대의 정책 컨트롤타워 기능이 제대로 작동하고 있는지 따져볼 필요가 있다. 이번 세제개편안에 국민이 크게 반발하는 것은 주거 현실을 도외시했기 때문이다. 어렵게 장만한 집 한 채를 세 주고 다른 곳에 거주할 수밖에 없는 국민, 은퇴 후 고정 소득이 없는 고령층까지 투기꾼 취급을 받고 징벌적 세금을 맞게 생겼다. 그 여파는 벌써 전월세를 사는 세입자에게도 번지고 있다. 세제가 부동산 대란의 불씨가 될 판이다. 정부와 여당은 지금이라도 세제 개편을 원점에서 재검토하는 게 맞다.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Tax Reform Package in Disarray Deserves Complete Overhaul
summaryTr: The government's tax reform plan has entered a complete review due to public backlash.
Elderly homeowners and non-residents strongly resisted punitive property holding taxes.
The absence of policy control functions at the Blue House has deepened confusion over real estate policy.
editorial.bodyTr: The backlash from the government's tax reform plan announced last week has been intense. Thousands of comments on proposed amendments to the Comprehensive Real Estate Tax Act and the Income Tax Act have been posted on the National Assembly's Citizens Participation Legislative Center. An unprecedented level of tax resistance has erupted immediately following the announcement of the tax reform package. Particularly fierce opposition has come from elderly residents of ultra-luxury homes in Gangnam and non-resident single-homeowners. For some ultra-luxury properties, annual property taxes could spike to tens of millions of won, making it difficult for elderly retirees who purchased their homes long ago to afford. Long-term homeowners among the elderly with no connection to speculation have every reason to be frustrated with such punitive property taxes. There is also complaint that the exceptional circumstances for non-resident single-homeowners—such as job transfers and medical treatment—that the government has outlined are overly restrictive. Some people have rented out their homes to support grandchildren while leasing housing near their children's residences, while others must leave their homes vacant for extended periods due to overseas work or studies. As the situation grew serious, Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yun-chul retreated, saying he would review non-resident exemption requirements with maximum flexibility. Individual Savings Accounts with reduced tax benefits and a "stock price suppression prevention" law that seems to run counter to legislative intent have faced pushback from younger generations. Ultimately, the plan drew criticism from President Lee Jae-myung and was sent back for comprehensive review. A tax reform package represents a major pillar of economic management, and with inter-party consultations already completed, it is highly unusual for a president to criticize a policy announcement just days later. Even within the ruling party, criticism has emerged, saying the finance ministry needs to get its act together. Coordination with the presidential office should have been completed before party-government consultations, so it is difficult to understand why the government is only now stepping forward belatedly. The presidential office's function as a policy control tower warrants scrutiny. The strong public backlash to this tax reform proposal stems from disregard for the nation's housing reality. Citizens forced to rent out homes they worked hard to acquire and live elsewhere, and elderly retirees without fixed income after retirement, now find themselves treated as speculators and facing punitive taxes. The fallout is already spreading to tenants struggling with monthly rent payments. This tax system threatens to become a spark for a real estate crisis. The government and ruling party should reconsider the tax reform package from scratch at this point.

editorial.title: Linking growth to jobs
editorial.body: Korea needs to restructure job market to drive growth beyond chip sector A country can have a record current-account surplus and still have too few jobs. South Korea is providing a fresh example of this awkward contradiction. Semiconductor exports are lifting growth forecasts toward 3 percent, while the labor market is losing momentum. The economy is accelerating on paper while slowing where people look for work. The state-run Korea Labor Institute cut its forecast for this year's increase in employment from 210,000 to 103,000 in a report released Thursday. It expects the employment rate to fall to 62.7 percent and the unemployment rate to rise to 2.9 percent. If those projections materialize, the employment rate will decline for the first time since the pandemic-stricken year of 2020. Falling employment and rising unemployment have coincided only four times since 2000. The weakness is especially troubling among young Koreans. Employment among people in their 20s has fallen for 44 consecutive months, while their employment rate dropped 1.3 percentage points in the first half from a year earlier. The decline is concentrated at the point of entry. The number of young people with three months or less on the job has fallen sharply, while new graduates have been hit harder than the broader age group. Demographics offer only part of the explanation. If population decline were the main culprit, the deterioration would be less concentrated among new entrants. Instead, a growing number of young job seekers are delaying graduation or remaining outside the job market as companies tend to favor experienced workers. The broader figures point to another imbalance. By industry, manufacturing shed 62,000 jobs in the first half. Services added 300,000 jobs, yet most of the increase came from health and social welfare, while professional, scientific and technical services lost 88,000. Meanwhile, regular employment grew at only one-third of last year's pace, and nonwage workers accounted for two-thirds of total employment growth. This is hardly the profile of a broad-based private-sector recovery. The Korea Labor Institute attributes the weak employment picture to the economy's heavy reliance on semiconductors, even as growth forecasts are being raised toward 3 percent. Chipmaking, after all, is highly capital-intensive and generates less than half as many jobs per unit of output as manufacturing overall. Since the increase in exports is largely driven by rising memory prices, the corresponding gain in physical output, which is more closely tied to employment, has been limited. Whether Korea’s job market can improve in the second half, therefore, depends on the recovery of domestic demand and sectors beyond semiconductors. State-led cash assistance and short-term public jobs can cushion a downturn, but they cannot create a healthy labor market. Policies should put greater weight on expanding the supply of quality jobs that can absorb workers over time. Services could be a good place to start. They account for more than 70 percent of employment and about 60 percent of GDP, yet Korea's service-sector labor productivity remains near the bottom of the OECD. The long-delayed service industry development bill deserves renewed attention, alongside regulatory reform that allows productive service businesses to expand. Artificial intelligence adds another dimension to the job-creation challenge. Korea has abundant technological capability, but technology becomes economically useful only when firms can turn it into products and services. Universities and research institutes need clearer routes to commercialization, while startups and smaller companies should have greater access to AI infrastructure. Semiconductors can remain Korea's main growth engine, at least for a while. They cannot, however, serve as the country's sole job provider. A healthy economy needs a transmission belt from productivity and exports to domestic demand and employment. Policymakers should repair that loop before another strong growth headline masks how little of the growth reaches workers’ paychecks. summaryTr: 남한 경제는 종이 위에서는 성장하지만 일자리 창출은 정체되어 있으며, 고용 전망이 거의 절반으로 단축되었다.
젊은 근로자들은 기업들이 신입보다 경험자를 선호하면서 44개월 연속 일자리 감소에 직면해 있다.
반도체 중심의 성장은 생산량당 더 적은 일자리를 창출하며, 한국은 고용을 지속하기 위해 서비스 및 인공지능 부문을 개발해야 한다.
editorial.bodyTr:
한국은 반도체 부문을 넘어 성장을 주도하기 위해 일자리 시장을 구조조정해야 한다

한 국가는 사상 최고의 경상수지 흑자를 기록하면서도 여전히 일자리가 부족할 수 있다. 대한민국이 이러한 어색한 모순의 신선한 사례를 제공하고 있다. 반도체 수출은 성장 전망을 3퍼센트 방향으로 끌어올리고 있는 반면, 노동시장은 모멘텀을 잃고 있다. 경제는 종이 위에서는 가속화되고 있지만 사람들이 일자리를 찾는 곳에서는 둔화되고 있다.

국책연구기관인 한국노동연구원은 목요일 발표한 보고서에서 올해 고용 증가 전망치를 21만 명에서 10만 3천 명으로 하향 조정했다. 고용률은 62.7퍼센트로 하락하고 실업률은 2.9퍼센트로 상승할 것으로 예상했다. 이러한 전망이 현실화되면 고용률은 팬데믹으로 인한 2020년 이후 처음으로 감소하게 될 것이다. 고용 감소와 실업 증가가 동시에 나타난 것은 2000년 이후 네 번뿐이다.

editorials.title: Linking growth to jobs
editorials.body: Korea needs to restructure job market to drive growth beyond chip sector A country can have a record current-account surplus and still have too few jobs. South Korea is providing a fresh example of this awkward contradiction. Semiconductor exports are lifting growth forecasts toward 3 percent, while the labor market is losing momentum. The economy is accelerating on paper while slowing where people look for work. The state-run Korea Labor Institute cut its forecast for this year's increase in employment from 210,000 to 103,000 in a report released Thursday. It expects the employment rate to fall to 62.7 percent and the unemployment rate to rise to 2.9 percent. If those projections materialize, the employment rate will decline for the first time since the pandemic-stricken year of 2020. Falling employment and rising unemployment have coincided only four times since 2000. The weakness is especially troubling among young Koreans. Employment among people in their 20s has fallen for 44 consecutive months, while their employment rate dropped 1.3 percentage points in the first half from a year earlier. The decline is concentrated at the point of entry. The number of young people with three months or less on the job has fallen sharply, while new graduates have been hit harder than the broader age group. Demographics offer only part of the explanation. If population decline were the main culprit, the deterioration would be less concentrated among new entrants. Instead, a growing number of young job seekers are delaying graduation or remaining outside the job market as companies tend to favor experienced workers. The broader figures point to another imbalance. By industry, manufacturing shed 62,000 jobs in the first half. Services added 300,000 jobs, yet most of the increase came from health and social welfare, while professional, scientific and technical services lost 88,000. Meanwhile, regular employment grew at only one-third of last year's pace, and nonwage workers accounted for two-thirds of total employment growth. This is hardly the profile of a broad-based private-sector recovery. The Korea Labor Institute attributes the weak employment picture to the economy's heavy reliance on semiconductors, even as growth forecasts are being raised toward 3 percent. Chipmaking, after all, is highly capital-intensive and generates less than half as many jobs per unit of output as manufacturing overall. Since the increase in exports is largely driven by rising memory prices, the corresponding gain in physical output, which is more closely tied to employment, has been limited. Whether Korea’s job market can improve in the second half, therefore, depends on the recovery of domestic demand and sectors beyond semiconductors. State-led cash assistance and short-term public jobs can cushion a downturn, but they cannot create a healthy labor market. Policies should put greater weight on expanding the supply of quality jobs that can absorb workers over time. Services could be a good place to start. They account for more than 70 percent of employment and about 60 percent of GDP, yet Korea's service-sector labor productivity remains near the bottom of the OECD. The long-delayed service industry development bill deserves renewed attention, alongside regulatory reform that allows productive service businesses to expand. Artificial intelligence adds another dimension to the job-creation challenge. Korea has abundant technological capability, but technology becomes economically useful only when firms can turn it into products and services. Universities and research institutes need clearer routes to commercialization, while startups and smaller companies should have greater access to AI infrastructure. Semiconductors can remain Korea's main growth engine, at least for a while. They cannot, however, serve as the country's sole job provider. A healthy economy needs a transmission belt from productivity and exports to domestic demand and employment. Policymakers should repair that loop before another strong growth headline masks how little of the growth reaches workers’ paychecks. summaryTr: A sanitation worker died alone while working in Seoul's Jongno district.

Abolishing the exception clause is essential to prevent repeated workplace deaths.
editorials.bodyTr: A sanitation worker died alone in the early morning hours while working in the heart of Seoul. While the principle is to work in teams of three, he ended up handling both vehicle operation and garbage collection by himself, leading to his tragic death. The law revised in 2019 following a series of industrial accident deaths among sanitation workers has been rendered powerless through loopholes created by "exceptional clauses." The privatization of sanitation work has resulted in severe labor shortages and cost-cutting measures that prioritize profit over worker safety. Companies have been systematically exploiting these exceptions to reduce staffing levels below legal requirements. The responsibility ultimately falls on the government agencies that fail to properly enforce these regulations and on companies that prioritize efficiency over human life. The death of yet another sanitation worker represents a clear failure of our system to protect vulnerable workers. We need immediate action to close these legal loopholes and strengthen enforcement mechanisms. The lives of those who keep our cities clean should not be sacrificed for corporate profits. It is time for the government to take decisive steps to ensure that all sanitation workers are provided with adequate staffing levels and safe working conditions, regardless of whether their employers are public or private entities.
